_comment: Topic queue for the auto-blog pipeline (scripts/blog/generate.mjs). Each run generates the next N items whose status is 'pending', writes a full SEO article to src/content/articles/<slug>.md dated that day, marks the item 'published', then the workflow rebuilds and deploys the site. Add items freely; keep slugs unique and matching no existing article. An item may instead carry a pre-written 'body' (+ optional 'faq'/'description') and it will be published verbatim with no LLM call.

posts.title: Why Do Athletes Choke Under Pressure? The Real Science
posts.primaryKeyword: why do athletes choke under pressure
posts.audience: athletes and coaches who want to understand the mechanism behind choking, not just be told to relax
posts.angle: Explain choking as a specific brain event: a skill that runs automatically gets hijacked by conscious attention (explicit monitoring / paralysis by analysis). Cover why high stakes trigger it, why elite performers show less prefrontal interference, and the three levers that reduce it (external focus, a pre-shot routine, pressure training). Point readers to the fix-focused companion article.
posts.protocol: external focus, articulatory suppression cue word

posts.title: How to Stop Being Nervous Before a Game
posts.primaryKeyword: how to stop being nervous before a game
posts.audience: athletes who get anxious, tight, or sick before they compete
posts.angle: You cannot delete nerves, and trying to makes them worse. Teach reframing arousal as readiness (excited vs calm-down), a fast breathing reset, a fixed pre-game routine, and shrinking attention to the next action. Give a clear numbered pre-game sequence.
posts.protocol: arousal reappraisal, physiological sigh, fixed routine

posts.title: The Physiological Sigh: The Fastest Way to Calm Down Before You Compete
posts.primaryKeyword: physiological sigh
posts.audience: athletes who need to drop their heart rate in seconds before a start, free throw, or serve
posts.angle: Explain the double-inhale-then-long-exhale pattern (research popularized by Andrew Huberman at Stanford) and why it calms the body faster than a slow breath. Give exact reps, when to use it, and how to make it a cue. Keep it precise and practical.

posts.title: Box Breathing for Athletes (The 4-4-4-4 Reset)
posts.primaryKeyword: box breathing for athletes
posts.audience: athletes who want a simple repeatable way to steady themselves under pressure
posts.angle: Teach the 4-4-4-4 pattern (inhale, hold, exhale, hold), why the even rhythm steadies the nervous system, and how to use it pre-game and between points. Compare it to the physiological sigh (box breathing to hold steady, the sigh to drop fast). Numbered how-to.

posts.title: What to Do the Night Before a Big Competition
posts.primaryKeyword: night before a competition
posts.audience: athletes who lie awake the night before and show up drained
posts.angle: A calm, boring, repeatable evening beats a hyped one. Cover gear prep the night before, a light visualization, a wind-down routine, phone and food rules, and accepting that a bad night's sleep will not wreck you (the worry does more damage than the lost hour). Numbered checklist.

posts.title: How to Build a Pre-Game Routine That Actually Works
posts.primaryKeyword: pre-game routine
posts.audience: athletes who want consistency and a way to trigger their best state on demand
posts.angle: A routine is a switch that tells your brain it is time to perform, and its power comes from being the same every time regardless of stakes. Cover the three layers (physical, visual, mental cue), building an anchor, and keeping it short enough to survive a chaotic warm-up. Give a build-your-own template.

posts.title: Process Goals vs Outcome Goals (With Examples for Athletes)
posts.primaryKeyword: process goals vs outcome goals
posts.audience: athletes and coaches who fixate on winning and tighten up because of it
posts.angle: Outcome goals (win, place, PR) are outside your control and spike pressure. Process goals (the two or three controllables this rep) keep you loose and actually raise the odds of the outcome. Give a clean method to convert any outcome goal into process goals, with sport examples.

posts.title: Pressure Training: How to Make Practice Harder Than the Game
posts.primaryKeyword: pressure training for athletes
posts.audience: athletes and coaches whose skills fall apart in competition despite great practices
posts.angle: Skills only choke when they were never truly automated under stress. Show how to add consequences, audiences, fatigue, and scoreboard pressure to practice so the game feels familiar. Give five concrete ways to manufacture pressure in training.

posts.title: Self-Distancing: Why Talking to Yourself by Name Calms You Down
posts.primaryKeyword: self-distancing self-talk
posts.audience: athletes who spiral in their own head during competition
posts.angle: Research by Ethan Kross shows that using your own name or 'you' instead of 'I' creates distance from the emotion and improves performance under stress. Explain why it works and how to build a third-person cue you can use mid-game. Practical scripts.

posts.title: Confidence Built on Evidence: The 5-Win Protocol
posts.primaryKeyword: how to build confidence in sports
posts.audience: athletes whose confidence rises and falls with results
posts.angle: Confidence from applause is fragile; confidence from evidence lasts. Teach a daily 5-Win log (three to five small controllable wins logged after every session) that builds a bank of proof your brain can draw on under pressure. Give the exact logging method.

posts.title: Should You Let Your Kid Quit Their Sport?
posts.primaryKeyword: should i let my child quit their sport
posts.audience: parents whose child suddenly wants to quit and who do not know whether to push or allow it
posts.angle: Separate 'I want to quit' the emotion from 'I want to quit' the decision. Give a framework: never decide right after a bad game, find the real reason (fear, a coach, burnout, social), honor a commitment to the season, then choose together. Warm, practical, no guilt.

posts.title: How to Talk to Your Kid's Coach (Without Being That Parent)
posts.primaryKeyword: how to talk to your child's coach
posts.audience: sports parents with a concern about playing time, roles, or treatment
posts.angle: There is a right way and a wrong time. Cover the 24-hour rule before raising anything, never doing it at the field, asking about your child's development not playing time, and the questions that build a partnership with the coach instead of a fight. Give a script.

posts.title: The Mental Game of Basketball: How to Stay Locked In
posts.primaryKeyword: mental game for basketball
posts.audience: basketball players who lose focus, rush shots, or fade late in games
posts.angle: Basketball punishes a wandering mind: fast transitions, free throws under silence, momentum swings. Cover a free-throw routine, an error-recovery cue after a turnover, next-play focus, and staying aggressive when behind. Sport-specific and concrete.

posts.title: How to Calm Your Nerves Before a Tennis Match
posts.primaryKeyword: how to calm nerves before a tennis match
posts.audience: tennis players who tighten up on serve, big points, and tiebreaks
posts.angle: Tennis is long stretches of thinking time between points, which feeds nerves. Cover a between-point routine (the four stages), a breathing reset on the changeover, a serve ritual, and playing the next point only. Sport-specific.

posts.title: How to Get Over the Fear of Failure in Sports
posts.primaryKeyword: fear of failure in sports
posts.audience: athletes who play not to lose instead of playing to win
posts.angle: Fear of failure makes you tentative, and tentative is how you actually fail. Cover redefining failure as data, detaching identity from results, playing for process, and a pre-game reframe. Distinct from the existing fear-of-failure piece by focusing on the play-not-to-lose trap and a concrete reframe drill.

posts.title: How to Refocus After a Mistake (The 3-Second Reset)
posts.primaryKeyword: how to refocus after a mistake
posts.audience: athletes who let one error snowball into three
posts.angle: One mistake only costs you if you keep paying for it. Teach a fast in-competition error-recovery routine: a physical trigger (glove tug, deep breath), a release word, and a next-action focus. Give the numbered 3-second reset and how to drill it.

posts.title: How to Beat the Yips in Golf (Stop Choking Over the Ball)
posts.primaryKeyword: how to beat the yips in golf
posts.audience: golfers whose smooth swing or putting stroke falls apart the moment it counts
posts.angle: The yips are explicit monitoring: a grooved motion gets hijacked by conscious control on the tee or the short putt. Explain the mechanism, then give the fixes that work in golf specifically: an external target focus, a quiet-eye pre-shot routine, a hold cue word through impact, and pressure practice on the range. Reference the choking science.
posts.protocol: quiet-eye routine, external target focus, cue word

posts.title: How to Make Free Throws Under Pressure
posts.primaryKeyword: how to make free throws under pressure
posts.audience: basketball players who shoot great in practice but miss free throws late in games
posts.angle: A free throw is the same shot every time, so misses under pressure are mental, not mechanical. Give a fixed free-throw routine (breath, dribble count, target, one cue), why the routine has to be identical regardless of score, and how to rehearse it under simulated pressure. Late-game, high-silence context specific to basketball.

posts.title: How to Build Confidence in Basketball
posts.primaryKeyword: how to build confidence in basketball
posts.audience: basketball players who hesitate, pass up open shots, or shrink when the game speeds up
posts.angle: Confidence in basketball is built on evidence and reps, not hype. Cover shooting your shot without hesitation, a short memory after a miss, a pre-game confidence routine, and logging small controllable wins. Address the hesitation-to-turnover spiral specific to hoops.

posts.title: How to Stop Choking in Tennis (Big Points and Double Faults)
posts.primaryKeyword: how to stop choking in tennis
posts.audience: tennis players who tighten up on big points, break points, and second serves
posts.angle: Tennis gives you too much time to think between points, which feeds choking on serve and big points. Cover a between-point routine, a serve ritual that survives pressure, external focus on the target not the mechanics, and playing the next point only. Double-fault spiral specific to tennis.
posts.protocol: between-point routine, serve ritual, next-point focus

posts.title: How to Handle Penalty Kick Pressure
posts.primaryKeyword: penalty kick pressure
posts.audience: soccer players who have to step up and take a penalty with everything on the line
posts.angle: A penalty is the purest pressure moment in soccer: you against the keeper, everyone watching. Cover deciding your side early and not changing, a fixed walk-up routine, breath control on the spot, and keeping your eyes off the keeper. The freeze-and-change-your-mind trap specific to penalties.

posts.title: How to Bounce Back After a Loss in Soccer
posts.primaryKeyword: how to bounce back after a loss in soccer
posts.audience: soccer players and teams who let one loss turn into a slump
posts.angle: One loss only costs you if you carry it into the next match and training week. Apply the 24-hour rule, extract one lesson, and reset team and individual confidence. Cover the mistake that snowballs during a match too (an error-recovery reset). Team-sport momentum context.

posts.title: Gymnastics Mental Blocks: How to Get Your Skills Back
posts.primaryKeyword: gymnastics mental block
posts.audience: gymnasts who suddenly cannot throw a skill they used to do, on beam, floor, or bars
posts.angle: A gymnastics mental block (lost move syndrome) is fear plus an overloaded conscious system balking at a skill. Explain why it happens, why forcing it makes it worse, and the ladder back: drills and numbers, breaking the skill down, controlling fear with breathing, and rebuilding trust rep by rep. Beam and vault fear specific to gymnastics.
posts.protocol: skill ladder, fear-reset breathing, trust reps

posts.title: How to Calm Pre-Race Nerves in Swimming
posts.primaryKeyword: pre-race nerves swimming
posts.audience: swimmers who get anxious and drained behind the blocks before a race
posts.angle: Swimming isolates you: no coach, no crowd, just you and the black line, so nerves have nowhere to go. Cover a behind-the-blocks routine, reframing nerves as readiness, a physiological sigh to drop the heart rate, and a race plan focused on splits not the clock. The isolation problem specific to swimming.
posts.protocol: behind-the-blocks routine, physiological sigh, split focus

posts.title: Mental Training for Distance Running (Push Through the Wall)
posts.primaryKeyword: mental training for distance running
posts.audience: distance runners who fade mentally when it hurts, in training and on race day
posts.angle: Endurance is a mental game once the legs are tired. Cover chunking the distance, associative vs dissociative focus and when to use each, a mantra for the pain cave, and calming race-morning nerves. The wall and the late-race mental fade specific to distance running.
posts.protocol: chunking, mantra, associative focus in the pain cave

posts.title: How to Control Fear in Boxing
posts.primaryKeyword: how to control fear in boxing
posts.audience: boxers who feel fear before and during a fight and want to use it, not freeze
posts.angle: Fear in boxing is rational and useful if you channel it. Cover reframing fight-night adrenaline as readiness, a walk-out and glove-touch routine, staying composed after getting hit (the panic-and-gas-out trap), and controlled breathing between rounds. Combat-specific fear management.
posts.protocol: adrenaline reframe, between-round breathing, get-hit reset

posts.title: How to Calm Nerves Before a Fight (BJJ, MMA, Wrestling)
posts.primaryKeyword: how to calm nerves before a fight
posts.audience: grapplers and fighters whose nerves spike in the days and minutes before competing
posts.angle: Competition nerves in combat sports peak in the bullpen before you walk out. Cover a warm-up and breathing routine, a game plan that gives the mind a job, reframing the adrenaline dump, and staying present instead of running the what-ifs. Weigh-in and bullpen context specific to combat sports.
posts.protocol: bullpen breathing, game-plan focus, adrenaline reframe

posts.title: How to Psych Up for a Max Lift (Without Wrecking Your Nerves)
posts.primaryKeyword: how to psych up for a big lift
posts.audience: lifters who either under-arouse or over-hype before a heavy single and miss it
posts.angle: A max lift needs the right arousal level: too flat and you are weak, too amped and you lose technique and burn out. Cover finding your arousal sweet spot, a consistent pre-lift routine and cue, controlled aggression, and one focus thought for the lift. The over-hype-and-miss trap specific to lifting.
posts.protocol: arousal sweet spot, pre-lift routine, one cue

posts.title: Should My Child Specialize in One Sport?
posts.primaryKeyword: should my child specialize in one sport
posts.audience: parents pressured to pick one sport early for their kid
posts.angle: Early specialization raises burnout and injury risk and rarely produces the pro outcome parents imagine. Cover what research says about multi-sport athletes, when specialization makes sense, and how to decide with your kid instead of for them.

posts.title: 7 Signs of Burnout in Young Athletes (and What to Do)
posts.primaryKeyword: signs of burnout in young athletes
posts.audience: parents worried their kid is losing the love of the game
posts.angle: Burnout shows up as dread, dropping performance, physical complaints, and pulling away. List the warning signs, the causes (over-scheduling, outcome pressure), and how to pull a kid back from the edge without making them quit.

posts.title: What to Say When Your Child Loses Their Starting Spot
posts.primaryKeyword: child lost starting position
posts.audience: parents whose kid got benched or demoted and is crushed
posts.angle: A demotion is a chance to build resilience if you handle it right. Cover validating the disappointment without bashing the coach, refocusing on controllables, and the words that help a benched kid come back stronger.

posts.title: Imposter Syndrome in Athletes: Why You Feel Like a Fraud
posts.primaryKeyword: imposter syndrome in athletes
posts.audience: athletes who succeed but feel they do not deserve it and wait to be exposed
posts.angle: Imposter syndrome hits high performers hardest. Explain why success can feel like luck, how it drives overtraining and anxiety, and concrete ways to internalize your wins (evidence logging, reframing, separating feeling from fact).

posts.title: How to Stop Comparing Yourself to Other Athletes
posts.primaryKeyword: stop comparing yourself to other athletes
posts.audience: athletes who lose confidence scrolling stats, highlights, and teammates
posts.angle: Comparison steals confidence and focus. Cover the comparison trap (especially social media), running your own race, competing against your past self, and a cue to redirect when the comparison spiral starts.

posts.title: Perfectionism in Sports: How to Let Go and Play Free
posts.primaryKeyword: perfectionism in sports
posts.audience: athletes whose fear of a mistake makes them tight and tentative
posts.angle: Perfectionism looks like high standards but plays like fear. It makes athletes cautious and unravels them after one error. Cover good vs bad perfectionism, chasing excellence not perfection, and freeing up by focusing on process and effort.

posts.title: The Mental Side of Injury Recovery for Athletes
posts.primaryKeyword: mental side of injury recovery
posts.audience: injured athletes struggling with identity, fear, and coming back
posts.angle: Injury is as much a mental battle as a physical one: lost identity, fear of reinjury, isolation. Cover keeping identity beyond sport, staged mental goals during rehab, visualization, and rebuilding trust in the body on return.

posts.title: How to Be a Mentally Tough Team Captain
posts.primaryKeyword: how to be a good team captain
posts.audience: captains and team leaders who set the emotional tone
posts.angle: A captain leads the mental game, not just the huddle. Cover staying composed when the team is rattled, holding standards, lifting teammates after mistakes, and being the steady emotional thermostat under pressure.

posts.title: How to Coach Mental Toughness (A Practical Guide)
posts.primaryKeyword: how to coach mental toughness
posts.audience: coaches who want to build the mental game, not just skills
posts.angle: Mental toughness is trained, not preached. Give coaches concrete methods: pressure practice, process language, how to debrief mistakes, building team confidence on evidence, and modeling composure.

posts.title: How to Stay Focused for a Full Soccer Match
posts.primaryKeyword: how to stay focused in soccer
posts.audience: soccer players who switch off, lose concentration, and get scored on late
posts.angle: A soccer match has long dull stretches that punish a wandering mind. Cover refocus cues after a mistake, staying switched on off the ball, resetting at set pieces, and finishing games mentally strong. Second-half concentration specific to soccer.

posts.title: How to Overcome a Slump in Tennis
posts.primaryKeyword: how to get out of a tennis slump
posts.audience: tennis players stuck in a losing streak or a confidence dip
posts.angle: A tennis slump is usually a confidence and focus problem, not a technique one. Cover breaking the losing-streak spiral, going back to process and one point at a time, rebuilding on small wins, and managing the between-match head. Individual-sport isolation specific to tennis.

posts.title: How to Improve Concentration in Golf
posts.primaryKeyword: how to improve concentration in golf
posts.audience: golfers who lose focus over a long round and drop shots late
posts.angle: Golf demands focus in short bursts across four-plus hours, then punishes lapses. Cover switching focus on and off between shots (conserve attention), a consistent pre-shot routine, staying present after a bad hole, and finishing the round mentally. Shot-by-shot focus specific to golf.
